# Overview



The Collective Variables Module (Colvars) is a high-performance software library designed for molecular simulation and analysis that provides a sophisticated implementation of sampling algorithms operating on a reduced space of continuously differentiable functions known as collective variables. First released in 2008 as part of NAMD version 2.7b1, Colvars has evolved into a mature, widely-adopted library integrated into major molecular dynamics packages including NAMD, LAMMPS, VMD, GROMACS, and Tinker-HP.

![Colvars logo](https://github.com/Colvars/colvars/blob/master/doc/logo/colvars-logo.svg?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L13)

## What Are Collective Variables?

Collective variables (CVs) are mathematical functions that describe complex structural and dynamical properties of molecular systems in a reduced-dimensional space. Unlike individual atomic coordinates, which can number in the thousands or millions for realistic biomolecular systems, CVs capture essential features such as distances between molecular centers of mass, dihedral angles, coordination numbers, root-mean-square deviations, and many other geometric or physical properties. This reduction enables efficient exploration of free energy landscapes and enhanced sampling techniques that would be computationally prohibitive in full-dimensional space.

The library provides a comprehensive framework for defining these variables through a flexible configuration language, applying various biasing potentials to drive sampling along chosen collective dimensions, and analyzing the resulting data to extract thermodynamic and kinetic information. The functionality includes free-energy estimators based on thermodynamic forces, non-equilibrium work calculations, and probability distribution analysis.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L9)

## Supported Simulation Engines

Colvars achieves engine independence through a well-designed proxy interface that abstracts the details of each molecular dynamics code. This architecture allows the same Colvars configuration files to work across different simulation packages with minimal modification, ensuring portability of research workflows.

| Engine | Integration Status | Configuration Method | Documentation |
|--------|-------------------|---------------------|---------------|
| **GROMACS** | Full support (2024+) | MDP file parameters | [GROMACS Manual](https://manual.gromacs.org/) |
| **LAMMPS** | Full support | Fix colvars command | [LAMMPS Download](https://lammps.sandia.gov/download.html) |
| **NAMD** | Native (original) | Config file directives | [NAMD Website](https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/namd/) |
| **Tinker-HP** | Full support | `.colvars` file | [Tinker-HP Website](https://tinker-hp.org/) |
| **VMD** | Full support | Tcl scripting | [VMD Website](https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/vmd/) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L15-L24)

## Core Capabilities

The Colvars library provides three fundamental categories of functionality that work together to enable advanced molecular simulations and analyses:

### Collective Variable Definitions

The library supports an extensive catalog of variable types covering common structural descriptors. These range from simple geometric quantities to complex protein-specific metrics and even custom neural network functions. The modular design allows combining multiple components into composite variables using arithmetic operations, enabling researchers to construct precisely the degrees of freedom needed for their specific scientific questions.

### Biasing and Sampling Methods

Building on the foundation of collective variables, Colvars implements numerous enhanced sampling algorithms. These include harmonic restraints and walls for simple confinement, Adaptive Biasing Force (ABF) for free energy surface reconstruction, various metadynamics variants for exploring rare events, umbrella integration techniques, and advanced methods like OPES (On-the-fly Probability Enhanced Sampling). Each method is implemented with careful attention to computational efficiency and numerical accuracy.

### Grid-Based Analysis

For methods that accumulate statistical information across collective variable space, Colvars provides robust grid infrastructure. This includes configurable grids with automatic handling of periodic and non-periodic boundaries, efficient algorithms for free energy surface integration from force data, and tools for custom multi-dimensional operations. The grid system supports both in-memory storage and efficient disk I/O for large-scale calculations.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L5-L9), [colvarbias.h](src/colvarbias.h#L22-L329), [colvargrid.h](src/colvargrid.h#L51-L995)

## Architecture Overview

The Colvars architecture follows a modular, object-oriented design that separates concerns into distinct layers with well-defined interfaces. This design facilitates maintenance, extensibility, and the integration with multiple simulation engines.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Simulation Engines"
        NAMD[NAMD]
        LAMMPS[LAMMPS]
        GROMACS[GROMACS]
        VMD[VMD]
    end
    
    subgraph "Proxy Interface Layer"
        COLVARPROXY[colvarproxy]
        ATOMS[colvarproxy_atoms]
        GROUPS[colvarproxy_atom_groups]
        SYSTEM[colvarproxy_system]
        SCRIPT[colvarproxy_script]
        SMP[colvarproxy_smp]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Colvars Module"
        MODULE[colvarmodule]
        CVARS[Collective Variables]
        BIASES[Biasing Methods]
        GRIDS[Grid Infrastructure]
    end
    
    subgraph "Collective Variable Components"
        CVC_DISTANCE[Distance CVCs]
        CVC_ANGLE[Angular CVCs]
        CVC_PROTEIN[Protein-Specific CVCs]
        CVC_CUSTOM[Custom/NN CVCs]
    end
    
    subgraph "Bias Implementations"
        BIAS_HARMONIC[Harmonic]
        BIAS_ABF[ABF]
        BIAS_META[Metadynamics]
        BIAS_OPES[OPES]
    end
    
    NAMD --> COLVARPROXY
    LAMMPS --> COLVARPROXY
    GROMACS --> COLVARPROXY
    VMD --> COLVARPROXY
    
    COLVARPROXY --> ATOMS
    COLVARPROXY --> GROUPS
    COLVARPROXY --> SYSTEM
    COLVARPROXY --> SCRIPT
    COLVARPROXY --> SMP
    
    ATOMS --> MODULE
    GROUPS --> MODULE
    SYSTEM --> MODULE
    SCRIPT --> MODULE
    SMP --> MODULE
    
    MODULE --> CVARS
    MODULE --> BIASES
    MODULE --> GRIDS
    
    CVARS --> CVC_DISTANCE
    CVARS --> CVC_ANGLE
    CVARS --> CVC_PROTEIN
    CVARS --> CVC_CUSTOM
    
    BIASES --> BIAS_HARMONIC
    BIASES --> BIAS_ABF
    BIASES --> BIAS_META
    BIASES --> BIAS_OPES
```

The architecture centers around the `colvarmodule` class ([src/colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L76-L960)), which serves as the main controller managing all Colvars components. The `colvarproxy` interface ([src/colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L549-L718)) abstracts communication with host simulation programs, handling tasks such as reading atomic coordinates, applying forces, and managing system parameters. Multiple specialized proxy subclasses handle specific concerns: atom management ([colvarproxy_atoms](src/colvarproxy.h#L44-L303)), atom group operations ([colvarproxy_atom_groups](src/colvarproxy.h#L305-L449)), parallel processing ([colvarproxy_smp](src/colvarproxy.h#L460-L510)), and scripting interfaces ([colvarproxy_script](src/colvarproxy.h#L514-L543)).

Collective variables are implemented through the `colvar` class ([src/colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L53-L722)), which aggregates one or more collective variable components (CVCs). Each CVC implements a specific mathematical function, such as distance or angle calculations, and provides derivatives with respect to atomic coordinates. This modular component system allows researchers to combine simple elements into complex collective variables.

Biasing methods derive from the base `colvarbias` class ([src/colvarbias.h](src/colvarbias.h#L22-L329)) and implement specific algorithms for applying forces to collective variables. Many biases use grids ([src/colvargrid.h](src/colvargrid.h#L51-L995)) to accumulate statistics, compute free energies, or store bias potentials. The grid system provides efficient multi-dimensional array operations with automatic handling of boundary conditions and periodic wrapping.

Sources: [colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L76-L960), [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L549-L718), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L53-L722)

## Project Structure

The Colvars repository is organized into logical directories containing source code, integration files for supported engines, documentation, examples, and testing infrastructure.

```
colvars/
├── src/                    # Core library source code
│   ├── colvarmodule.*      # Main controller class
│   ├── colvar.*            # Collective variable implementation
│   ├── colvarbias.*        # Base biasing class and derivatives
│   ├── colvarcomp.*        # Collective variable components
│   ├── colvargrid.*        # Grid infrastructure
│   ├── colvarproxy.*       # Proxy interface classes
│   └── colvarscript.*      # Scripting interface
├── namd/                   # NAMD-specific integration
├── lammps/                 # LAMMPS-specific integration
├── gromacs/                # GROMACS-specific integration
├── vmd/                    # VMD-specific integration
├── examples/               # Configuration examples
├── tests/                  # Test suites
├── doc/                    # Documentation files
└── devel-tools/            # Development utilities
```

The source directory contains the complete library implementation with clear separation between core functionality and engine-specific code. The integration directories contain patches and interface code required to incorporate Colvars into each supported simulation package. Examples and tests provide practical guidance and ensure numerical accuracy through continuous validation.

Sources: [Repository root structure](.), [src directory](src)

## Example Configuration

A basic Colvars configuration demonstrates the simplicity of the system. The following example defines a distance variable between two groups of atoms and applies a harmonic restraint:

```
colvar {                                    # Define a new variable
  name d                                    # Must give a name
  width 0.2                                  # Estimated fluctuation amplitude
  distance {                                 # Distance between COMs
    group1 { atomNumbers 1 2 3 }            # First atom group
    group2 { atomNumbers 4 5 6 }            # Second atom group
  }
}

harmonic {                                  # Define harmonic potential
  colvars d                                 # Apply to variable "d"
  centers 5.0                               # Center position
  forceConstant 10.0                        # Force constant
}
```

This configuration demonstrates key concepts: variable definition with naming and physical parameters, atom group specification, component selection, and bias application. The same syntax works across all supported simulation engines, promoting reproducibility and portability.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L52-L67)

## Key Features

The library provides numerous features designed for both usability and computational efficiency:

**Flexible Variable Definition**: Support for atomic groups defined by atom numbers, residue numbers, and atom names enables precise control over which atoms participate in collective variables. Named atom groups can be reused across multiple variables, reducing configuration complexity.

**Extended Lagrangian Dynamics**: For variables with rough energy landscapes, the library implements an extended Lagrangian formalism where the collective variable becomes a dynamic degree of freedom with its own effective mass and friction. This can significantly improve sampling efficiency and numerical stability.

**Parallel Computing**: Through the `colvarproxy_smp` interface, the library supports multi-threaded parallel execution. Different parallelization strategies are available, including distributing collective variable component calculations across threads and parallelizing bias evaluations.

**State Management**: Complete simulation state can be saved and restored through restart files, enabling long simulations to be interrupted and resumed without loss of information. State files include all variables, biases, grids, and internal counters.

**Output and Analysis**: The library produces comprehensive trajectory files with configurable output frequency, allowing detailed analysis of variable evolution. Additional analysis capabilities include autocorrelation functions, running averages, and probability distribution calculations.

**Scripting Interface**: For advanced control, scripting interfaces (particularly Tcl) allow real-time modification of bias parameters, custom force calculations, and complex workflow automation beyond what's possible through configuration files alone.

Sources: [colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L85-L960), [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L460-L543)

## Installation and Integration

Colvars can be obtained through multiple channels. The simplest approach is to use the version bundled with your preferred simulation engine. For access to the latest features and bug fixes, the library can be updated independently using the provided `update-colvars-code.sh` script.

To update Colvars in an existing simulation package source tree:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/Colvars/colvars.git
cd colvars
./update-colvars-code.sh /path/to/simulation/engine
```

This script copies the current Colvars source code into the target directory, preserving integration patches. After updating, recompile the simulation engine following its standard build procedure.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L92-L108)

## Learning Path

For developers and users new to Colvars, the recommended progression through the documentation ensures a solid foundation before tackling advanced topics:

1. **[Quick Start](2-quick-start)**: Get up and running with a simple example configuration
2. **[Installation and Integration](3-installation-and-integration)**: Detailed setup instructions for each supported engine
3. **[Basic Configuration Syntax](4-basic-configuration-syntax)**: Understanding the Colvars configuration language

After mastering the basics, dive into specialized areas:

- **Collective Variable Components**: Learn about distance variables, angular measures, coordination numbers, protein-specific variables, and custom neural network functions
- **Biasing Methods**: Explore harmonic restraints, ABF, metadynamics, umbrella integration, and OPES
- **Grid Operations**: Understand grid configuration, free energy integration, and multi-dimensional operations
- **Advanced Topics**: Proxy interfaces, atom group management, extended Lagrangian dynamics, parallel computing, and scripting

The modular nature of the documentation allows you to focus on the techniques most relevant to your research while developing a comprehensive understanding of the library's capabilities.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L28-L33)

# Quick Start


Welcome to the Colvars quick-start guide. This page helps you run your first collective variable simulation in minutes, with minimal configuration. You will learn how to enable Colvars in your MD engine, define a simple distance collective variable, apply a harmonic restraint, and understand the basic user-facing workflow. For deeper concepts, see the subsequent pages such as [Installation and Integration](3-installation-and-integration) and [Basic Configuration Syntax](4-basic-configuration-syntax).
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L148)

## User-facing architecture and workflow
The workflow you will follow involves enabling Colvars in your engine, providing a configuration file, and analyzing the output. Colvars does not require you to build its library yourself if you use supported, pre-compiled engines. During the simulation, Colvars periodically evaluates collective variables and applies biases according to your configuration, then writes output files.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Enable Colvars in MD engine] --> B[Provide configuration file]
  B --> C[Simulation loop: CV evaluation and bias application]
  C --> D[Write output files]
  D --> E[Post-process trajectories]
  E --> F[Visualize and analyze]
  A -->|Options| G[NAMD]
  A -->|Options| H[LAMMPS]
  A -->|Options| I[GROMACS 2024+]
  A -->|Options| J[VMD]
  A -->|Options| K[Tinker-HP]
```
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L26-L58)

## Project structure overview
Key directories and files in the Colvars repository that you will encounter or use.

- examples/ — Standalone example configurations illustrating common use cases.
- tests/ — Functional test configurations used for validation and reference snippets.
- doc/ — Reference manuals and documentation resources.
- colvartools/ — Post-processing scripts to work with Colvars output (e.g., histograms, free energy surfaces).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L10), [colvartools/README.md](/colvartools/README.md#L1-L17)

## Step 1: Choose and enable an engine
If you already have a supported engine installed (GROMACS 2024+, LAMMPS, NAMD, Tinker-HP, or VMD), enable Colvars in the engine’s configuration and provide the Colvars configuration file.

- NAMD: set colvars on and use cv configfile <file>.
- LAMMPS: use fix Colvars all colvars configfile <file>.
- GROMACS 2024+: in the .mdp file set colvars-active = yes and colvars-configfile = <file>.
- VMD: use cv molid top and cv configfile <file> (or the Colvars Dashboard plugin).
- Tinker-HP: use a configuration file with the same prefix as the .key file and extension .colvars.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L26-L58)

## Step 2: Write a minimal configuration
Create a Colvars configuration file that defines a collective variable and a bias. The following example defines a distance between two groups of atoms and applies a harmonic restraint.

### Minimal configuration example (works across engines)

```colvars
colvar {
  name d
  width 0.2
  distance {
    group1 { atomNumbers 1 2 3 }
    group2 { atomNumbers 4 5 6 }
  }
}

harmonic {
  colvars d
  centers 5.0
  forceConstant 10.0
}
```
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L63-L82)

## Step 3: Run and inspect output
After running your simulation with the Colvars configuration, check for the generated output files. Common outputs include trajectory files and state files written according to Colvars settings. These can be plotted or processed with the post-processing tools in colvartools/.
Sources: [colvartools/README.md](/colvartools/README.md#L1-L17), [README.md](/README.md#L26-L58)

## Learning from examples
The examples/ directory contains ready-to-use configurations that demonstrate various features. Below are two simplified examples you can adapt to your system. For complete, ready-to-run input decks, see the Colvars examples repository.

### Restrain NOE distances (protein-ligand example)
This example defines two distance-based variables and applies harmonic walls.

```colvars
colvar {
  name NOE_1
  distanceInv {
    exponent 6
    group1 {
      psfSegID PRA
      atomNameResidueRange HB1 2-2
      atomNameResidueRange HB2 2-2
      atomNameResidueRange HB3 2-2
    }
    group2 {
      psfSegID PRA
      atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
    }
  }
}

colvar {
  name NOE_2
  distanceInv {
    exponent 6
    group1 {
      psfSegID PRA PRB PRC PRD
      atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
      atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
      atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
      atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
    }
    group2 {
      psfSegID DRUG
      atomNameResidueRange H102 1-1
    }
  }
}

harmonicWalls {
  name walls_NOE
  colvars NOE_1 NOE_2
  lowerWalls 3.5 4.2
  lowerWallConstant 30.0
  upperWalls 4.5 4.9
  upperWallConstant 20.0
}
```
Sources: [examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in](/examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in#L1-L58)

### Restrain protein backbone orientation (simple example)
This example restrains the orientation of a protein backbone segment using a reference structure.

```colvars
colvarsTrajFrequency 100

colvar {
  name Orient
  orientation {
    atoms {
      psfSegID P
      atomNameResidueRange CA 20-350
    }
    refPositionsFile ref.pdb
  }
}

harmonic {
  colvars Orient
  centers (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
  forceConstant 500.
}
```
Sources: [examples/03_orientation.colvars.in](/examples/03_orientation.colvars.in#L1-L24)

> [!TIP]
> Always ensure your atom selections match the structure you are simulating. Use PDB/index files or explicit segment/residue naming to avoid selection errors.

# Installation and Integration



This page provides a comprehensive guide for installing and integrating the Colvars module with various molecular dynamics engines. Whether you prefer pre-built packages or custom compilation, this guide covers all installation methods and system requirements for beginner-level developers.

![Colvars logo](https://github.com/Colvars/colvars/blob/master/doc/logo/colvars-logo.svg?raw=true)

## Installation Overview

The Colvars module offers multiple installation pathways depending on your needs and technical expertise. You can either use pre-compiled versions distributed with supported MD packages or integrate the latest source code directly into your build environment. The module uses a proxy interface pattern to abstract engine-specific implementations while maintaining a unified API for collective variable calculations across different simulation backends.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L50)

### Installation Methods

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Installation Choice] --> B{Installation Method}
    B -->|Beginner| C[Pre-built Package]
    B -->|Advanced| D[Source Integration]
    B -->|Custom Build| E[Standalone CMake]
    
    C --> C1[GROMACS]
    C --> C2[LAMMPS]
    C --> C3[NAMD]
    C --> C4[VMD]
    C --> C5[Tinker-HP]
    
    D --> D1[update-colvars-code.sh]
    D1 --> D2[Patches Engine Sources]
    
    E --> E1[CMake Configuration]
    E1 --> E2[Build Options]
    E2 --> E3[MPI/TCL/Torch Support]
    
    C1 --> F[Verify Installation]
    C2 --> F
    C3 --> F
    C4 --> F
    D2 --> F
    E3 --> F
```

## Pre-Built Package Installation

The simplest approach for beginners is to use the pre-compiled versions of Colvars included with major simulation packages. This requires no additional compilation and provides immediate access to Colvars functionality through each engine's standard build process.

### Supported Simulation Engines

| Engine | Installation Method | Colvars Version Detection | Documentation Link |
|--------|---------------------|---------------------------|-------------------|
| **GROMACS** | Standard package installation | Version table on wiki | [GROMACS Manual](https://manual.gromacs.org/) |
| **LAMMPS** | Standard package installation | Version table on wiki | [LAMMPS Download](https://lammps.sandia.gov/download.html) |
| **NAMD** | Standard package installation | Version table on wiki | [NAMD Website](https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/namd/) |
| **VMD** | Standard package installation | Version table on wiki | [VMD Website](https://www.ks.uiuc.edu/Research/vmd/) |
| **Tinker-HP** | Standard package installation | Version table on wiki | [Tinker-HP Website](https://tinker-hp.org/) |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L14-L25)

### Pre-Built Configuration Example

After installing any supported package, you can immediately use Colvars with minimal configuration. For example, in LAMMPS:

```bash
# Create a simple Colvars configuration file
cat > colvars.inp << EOF
colvar {
  name d
  width 0.2
  distance {
    group1 { atomNumbers 1 2 3 }
    group2 { atomNumbers 4 5 6 }
  }
}

harmonic {
  colvars d
  centers 5.0
  forceConstant 10.0
}
EOF

# Run LAMMPS with Colvars
lmp -in input.lammps -var style colvars -var configfile colvars.inp
```

> [!TIP]
> The configuration syntax is identical across all supported engines, making it easy to transfer simulations between packages. Only the activation commands differ slightly between engines.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L62)

## Source Code Integration Using update-colvars-code.sh

For developers needing the latest features or custom builds, the `update-colvars-code.sh` script provides automated integration with any supported MD engine source tree. This script handles file copying, patching, and dependency management through a unified interface.

### Obtaining the Source Code

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/Colvars/colvars.git
cd colvars

# Or download the master branch
wget https://github.com/Colvars/colvars/archive/master.zip
unzip master.zip
cd colvars-master
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L70-L77)

### Script Usage and Options

The update script supports multiple engines with automatic detection and error handling:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Basic usage syntax
./update-colvars-code.sh [-f] <target source tree>

# Update LAMMPS source tree
./update-colvars-code.sh /path/to/lammps

# Update NAMD source tree (force mode)
./update-colvars-code.sh -f /path/to/NAMD_X.YY_Source

# Update VMD source tree
./update-colvars-code.sh /path/to/vmd-X.Y.Z

# Update GROMACS source tree (2024+ only)
./update-colvars-code.sh /path/to/gromacs
```

**Options:**
- `-f`: Force update mode - overwrites conflicting files like Makefiles
- `-R`: Reverse mode - updates git tree from downstream (undocumented)
- `--diff`: Comparison-only mode without modifications

Sources: [update-colvars-code.sh](update-colvars-code.sh#L8-L30)

### Engine Detection Logic

The script automatically identifies the target engine using specific signature files:

```bash
# Detection hierarchy
if [ -f "${target}/src/lammps.h" ]; then
  code="LAMMPS"
elif [ -f "${target}/src/NamdTypes.h" ]; then
  code="NAMD"
elif [ -f "${target}/src/VMDApp.h" ]; then
  code="VMD"
elif [ -f "${target}/include/molfile_plugin.h" ]; then
  code="VMD-PLUGINS"
elif [ -f "${target}/src/gromacs/version.h.cmakein" ]; then
  code="GROMACS"
fi
```

Sources: [update-colvars-code.sh](update-colvars-code.sh#L42-L60)

### GROMACS-Specific Integration

GROMACS 2024 and later use an MDModules interface requiring special handling:

```bash
# The script automatically checks for GROMACS version support
if [ ${code} == "GROMACS" ] ; then
  if [ ! -f ${target}/src/gromacs/applied_forces/colvars/colvarsMDModule.cpp ] ; then
    echo "ERROR: Versions of GROMACS prior to 2024 are no longer supported."
    exit 1
  fi
fi

# Copies files to: src/external/colvars/
# Applies patches to CMakeLists.txt
# Copies MDModules to: src/gromacs/applied_forces/colvars/
```

Sources: [update-colvars-code.sh](update-colvars-code.sh#L63-L70)

> [!TIP]
> For GROMACS 2024+, the update script automatically downloads and integrates the Lepton library (used for custom function parsing) unless you set `UPDATE_LEPTON=no` before running the script.

Sources: [update-colvars-code.sh](update-colvars-code.sh#L495-L520)

## Standalone CMake Build

For maximum flexibility or developing custom integrations, you can build Colvars as a standalone library using CMake. This approach allows fine-grained control over compilation options and dependency management.

### Basic Build Process

```bash
# Navigate to CMake directory
cd cmake

# Configure with default options (C++11 standard)
cmake ..

# Build the library
make

# Install (optional)
sudo make install
```

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L15)

### CMake Configuration Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD` | `11` | C++ language standard (11, 14, 17) |
| `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS` | `OFF` | Build shared libraries instead of static |
| `WARNINGS_ARE_ERRORS` | `OFF` | Treat compiler warnings as errors |
| `COLVARS_DEBUG` | `OFF` | Build with debugging symbols and no optimization |
| `ADDRESS_SANITIZER` | `OFF` | Enable address sanitizer for memory debugging |
| `COLVARS_LEPTON` | Auto | Build and link Lepton library for custom functions |
| `COLVARS_OPENMP` | `ON` | Enable (limited) OpenMP support |
| `COLVARS_MPI` | `OFF` | Link against MPI library |
| `COLVARS_TCL` | `OFF` | Link against Tcl library for scripting |
| `COLVARS_TORCH` | `OFF` | Link against PyTorch for neural network variables |
| `BUILD_TESTS` | `ON` | Build test suite |
| `ENABLE_COVERAGE` | `OFF` | Enable code coverage reporting |

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L20-L100)

### Advanced Configuration Examples

```bash
# Build with MPI and Torch support (requires C++17)
cmake -DCOLVARS_MPI=ON \
      -DCOLVARS_TORCH=ON \
      -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=17 \
      -DLIBTORCH_PREFIX=/path/to/libtorch \
      ..

# Build with address sanitizer for debugging
cmake -DADDRESS_SANITIZER=ON \
      -DCOLVARS_DEBUG=ON \
      ..

# Build with custom Tcl installation
cmake -DCOLVARS_TCL=ON \
      -DTCL_DIR=/usr/local/tcl8.6 \
      ..
```

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L102-L170)

### Compiler-Specific Options

The CMake configuration includes compiler-specific optimizations and warnings:

```cmake
# GNU/Clang/Intel compilers
target_compile_options(colvars PRIVATE -Wall -pedantic)

# MSVC (Visual Studio)
target_compile_options(colvars PRIVATE /Zc:__cplusplus /W3 /wd4244 /wd4267)

# Clang version-specific features
if(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_ID STREQUAL "Clang")
  if(CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER_VERSION GREATER 6)
    target_compile_options(colvars PRIVATE -Wshadow-field)
  endif()
endif()
```

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L52-L68)

## Engine-Specific Integration Details

Each MD engine integrates Colvars through a proxy class that implements the interface defined in `colvarproxy.h`. The following sections provide detailed integration patterns for each supported engine.

### LAMMPS Integration

LAMMPS uses a `fix` style interface to embed Colvars functionality:

```cpp
// LAMMPS fix command syntax
fix ID group-ID colvars configfile keyword value ...

// Example usage
fix Colvars all colvars colvars.inp output myjob
fix_modify Colvars tstat NPT
fix_modify Colvars seed 12345
```

**Key Features:**
- Accelerator variant: `colvars/kk` for KOKKOS support
- Supports restart files for continuing simulations
- Provides temperature coupling with LAMMPS thermostats
- Optional coordinate unwrapping

Sources: [lammps/doc/src/fix_colvars.rst](lammps/doc/src/fix_colvars.rst#L6-L50)

### NAMD Integration

NAMD uses the GlobalMaster mechanism to apply Colvars forces:

```cpp
// NAMD configuration
colvars on
cv configfile my_config.colvars
```

**Build Integration:**
- Apply `Makefile.patch` to NAMD's Makefile
- Add Lepton library dependency
- Includes custom CUDA integration through `cudaglobalmaster` proxy

Sources: [namd/Makefile.patch](namd/Makefile.patch#L1-L14), [namd/src/colvarproxy_namd.h](namd/src/colvarproxy_namd.h#L37-L84)

### GROMACS Integration

GROMACS 2024+ uses the MDModules framework:

```bash
# GROMACS 2024+ configuration (in .mdp file)
colvars-active = yes
colvars-configfile = my_config.colvars
```

**Build Integration:**
- Copies library to `src/external/colvars/`
- Applies CMake patches for build system integration
- Integrates with MDModule interface in `src/gromacs/applied_forces/colvars/`
- Automatically includes Lepton library for custom function support

Sources: [update-colvars-code.sh](update-colvars-code.sh#L495-L588)

### VMD Integration

VMD provides both a Tcl scripting interface and a graphical dashboard:

```tcl
# VMD Tcl interface
cv molid top
cv configfile my_config.colvars

# Or use the Colvars Dashboard plugin
package require cv_dashboard
```

**Build Integration:**
- Requires C++11 patch for modern architectures
- Includes the Colvars Dashboard plugin for visual configuration
- Provides additional analysis scripts in `vmd/scripts/`

Sources: [README-c++11.md](README-c++11.md#L18-L29)

## C++ Language Requirements

Colvars requires **C++11** as the minimum language standard across all supported platforms. This ensures compatibility with modern compilers while maintaining broad support for existing installations.

### Engine-Specific Standards

| Engine | C++ Standard | Notes |
|--------|--------------|-------|
| **GROMACS** | C++17 | Follows GROMACS requirements |
| **LAMMPS** | C++11 | Standard LAMMPS requirement |
| **NAMD** | C++11 | Standard NAMD requirement |
| **VMD** | C++11 (with patch) | Requires external patch for C++11 support |

Sources: [README-c++11.md](README-c++11.md#L18-L29)

### Compiler Compatibility

The following compilers and versions are supported:

- **GCC**: 4.8+ (C++11 support), 7+ recommended
- **Clang**: 3.3+ (C++11 support), 6.0+ recommended
- **Intel C++**: 15.0+ (C++11 support)
- **MSVC**: 2015+ (partial support, some features disabled)

> [!TIP]
> Very old compilers (e.g., GCC 4.4 on CentOS 6) are no longer supported as they are past end-of-life. Upgrade your compiler if you encounter build errors related to C++11 features.

Sources: [README-c++11.md](README-c++11.md#L10-L16)

# Basic Configuration Syntax



This page provides a comprehensive guide to the fundamental configuration syntax used by the Colvars module. Understanding these syntax fundamentals is essential before diving into specific collective variable types or biasing methods. The Colvars configuration system uses a keyword-based, block-structured format that is consistent across all supported molecular simulation engines (NAMD, LAMMPS, VMD, GROMACS, Tinker-HP).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L100), [colvarparse.h](src/colvarparse.h#L1-L100)

## Configuration File Structure Overview

![Colvars logo](doc/logo/colvars-logo.svg)

The Colvars configuration system is built on a hierarchical block structure where each logical component is defined within its own named block. The parser operates by reading keyword-value pairs and matching braces to delineate configuration blocks. At the highest level, configuration files contain definitions for collective variables (`colvar` blocks), biases or restraints (e.g., `harmonic`, `harmonicWalls`), and global settings that control overall behavior.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Colvars Configuration File] --> B[Global Settings]
    A --> C[Colvar Definitions]
    A --> D[Bias/Restraint Definitions]
    
    C --> C1[colvar block]
    C1 --> C2[Variable Type]
    C1 --> C3[Atom Groups]
    C1 --> C4[Parameters]
    
    D --> D1[harmonic block]
    D --> D2[harmonicWalls block]
    D --> D3[abf block]
    D --> D4[metadynamics block]
    
    C3 --> C4a[group1 block]
    C3 --> C5[group2 block]
```

The configuration parser recognizes keywords based on their isolation by whitespace or block delimiters, ensuring that keywords appearing as substrings within other values are not incorrectly interpreted. This robust parsing system supports multiple data types including scalars, vectors, strings, and boolean values, with automatic type conversion and validation.

Sources: [colvarparse.h](src/colvarparse.h#L30-L100), [colvarparse.cpp](src/colvarparse.cpp#L650-L750)

## Keyword-Value Pair Syntax

The fundamental building block of Colvars configuration is the keyword-value pair. Keywords are case-insensitive strings that identify specific configuration parameters, followed by one or more whitespace characters and then the corresponding value. Values can be scalar numbers, strings, booleans, or collections enclosed in braces for multi-line definitions.

**Scalar Values**: Simple numeric or string assignments follow the format `keyword value`. For example: `forceConstant 10.0` or `name myVariable`. The parser automatically converts string representations to appropriate numeric types (integers, real numbers) based on the expected parameter type. Boolean values accept multiple representations including `on/off`, `yes/no`, and `true/false`.

**Vector Values**: Multiple values for the same keyword can be provided space-separated. For example: `lowerWalls 3.5 4.2` defines two lower wall values corresponding to two collective variables. The parser reads all values until the end of the line or the start of a new keyword.

**String Values**: String values containing spaces should be enclosed in quotes, though this is rarely needed in practice as most string parameters (like atom selections) use their own internal parsing mechanisms.

> [!TIP]
> The parser performs strict validation of keyword names and will generate errors if unknown keywords are encountered within a configuration block. This helps catch typos and misconfigurations early.

Sources: [colvarparse.cpp](src/colvarparse.cpp#L150-L300), [colvarparse.cpp](src/colvarparse.cpp#L450-L550)

## Block Structure and Nesting

Configuration blocks are delimited by curly braces (`{` and `}`) and provide a hierarchical organization for related parameters. Each block begins with a block type identifier (like `colvar`, `harmonic`, `group1`) followed by an opening brace. The block contents contain keyword-value pairs defining properties specific to that block, and the block ends with a matching closing brace.

**Block Nesting**: Blocks can be nested to arbitrary depth. For example, a `colvar` block contains a variable type block (like `distance`), which in turn contains two `group1` and `group2` blocks for defining atom groups. The parser correctly handles nested braces by tracking brace counts and ensuring proper matching.

**Whitespace Insensitivity**: The parser is largely insensitive to whitespace formatting. Newlines, tabs, and spaces can be used interchangeably for indentation and readability. However, keywords and their values must be separated by at least one whitespace character.

Here's a complete example showing nested block structure:

```
colvar {
  name distance_AB
  distance {
    group1 {
      atomNumbers 1 2 3
    }
    group2 {
      atomNumbers 4 5 6
    }
  }
  width 0.2
}
```

The block type identifier (`colvar`, `distance`, `group1`) is itself a keyword that the parser uses to determine what parameters are valid within that block.

Sources: [colvarparse.cpp](src/colvarparse.cpp#L700-L850), [examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in](examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in#L1-L30)

## Comments in Configuration Files

Comments are essential for documenting configuration files and are supported through two primary mechanisms. Line comments begin with the `#` character and continue to the end of the line. Everything following the `#` on that line is ignored by the parser.

```
# This is a comment explaining the purpose of this block
colvar {
  name myVariable  # Inline comments are also supported
  width 0.2
}
```

Comments can appear anywhere in the configuration file and are particularly useful for documenting complex atom selections, parameter choices, or the scientific rationale behind specific configurations. The parser strips comments during the keyword validation process, so commented-out keywords do not trigger unknown keyword warnings.

> [!TIP]
> Use descriptive comments in your configuration files, especially when defining atom groups or setting specific force constants. This documentation becomes invaluable when revisiting simulations months later or sharing configurations with collaborators.

Sources: [colvarparse.cpp](src/colvarparse.cpp#L600-L650), [examples/02_aggregation.colvars.in](examples/02_aggregation.colvars.in#L1-L10)

## Global Configuration Options

Global options appear at the top level of the configuration file (outside any block) and control overall behavior of the Colvars module. These settings affect things like output frequency, analysis options, and restart file handling.

**Common Global Keywords**:

| Keyword | Description | Example |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| `colvarsTrajFrequency` | How often to write colvar values to trajectory file | `colvarsTrajFrequency 100` |
| `colvarsRestartFrequency` | How often to write restart files | `colvarsRestartFrequency 1000` |
| `analysis` | Enable analysis tasks (correlation functions, running averages) | `analysis on` |

Global options are typically placed at the beginning of the configuration file for clarity, though their position does not affect functionality. These options are parsed first and establish the framework within which individual colvars and biases operate.

```
colvarsTrajFrequency 100
colvarsRestartFrequency 1000
analysis on

colvar {
  # ... colvar definition
}
```

Sources: [examples/02_aggregation.colvars.in](examples/02_aggregation.colvars.in#L1-L2), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L450-L470)

## Collective Variable Block Syntax

The `colvar` block defines a single collective variable and is the most fundamental configuration block in Colvars. Every colvar must have a unique `name` parameter that identifies it within the simulation and allows biases to reference it.

**Required Parameters**: Every `colvar` block must specify a variable type (the specific collective variable function) and the necessary atom groups or reference data for that type. The `name` and `width` parameters are also essential.

```
colvar {
  name myDistance        # Unique identifier for this variable
  width 0.2             # Characteristic scale for this variable
  distance {             # Variable type
    group1 {
      atomNumbers 1 2 3
    }
    group2 {
      atomNumbers 4 5 6
    }
  }
}
```

**Optional Parameters**: Colvars support many optional parameters that modify behavior including:
- `lowerBoundary` and `upperBoundary`: Define valid range
- `period` and `wrapCenter`: For periodic variables
- `extendedLagrangian`: Enable extended dynamics
- `outputValue`, `outputVelocity`, `outputSystemForce`: Control what gets written to output

The `width` parameter is particularly important as it defines the characteristic fluctuation scale of the variable. This value is used internally by metadynamics (for Gaussian widths) and ABF (for grid spacing), making it a critical parameter for enhanced sampling methods.

Sources: [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L55-L95), [README.md](README.md#L60-L80), [examples/03_orientation.colvars.in](examples/03_orientation.colvars.in#L1-L15)

## Atom Group Definition Syntax

Atom groups are defined within blocks named `group1`, `group2`, or simply `group` depending on the variable type. These blocks specify which atoms participate in the collective variable calculation using flexible atom selection methods.

**Atom Selection Methods**: Multiple methods can be combined within a single group block:

| Selection Method | Syntax | Example |
|------------------|--------|---------|
| By atom number | `atomNumbers` | `atomNumbers 1 2 3` |
| By residue range | `atomNameResidueRange` | `atomNameResidueRange CA 20-350` |
| By PDB file | `atomsfile` + `atomsCol` | `atomsfile atoms.pdb; atomsCol B` |
| By segment | `psfSegID` | `psfSegID PRA` |
| Multiple selections | Repeat keywords | Multiple `atomNameResidueRange` lines |

```
group1 {
  # Select alpha carbons from residues 20-350
  psfSegID P
  atomNameResidueRange CA 20-350
}

group2 {
  # Select from PDB file based on beta column
  atomsfile atoms.pdb
  atomsCol B
  atomsColValue 1
}
```

**Ambiguous Atom Definitions**: When multiple atoms satisfy selection criteria, they are all included in the group. This is useful for handling ambiguous assignments like methyl group hydrogen atoms. For example, the NOE restraint example demonstrates handling ambiguous proton assignments:

```
group1 {
  # ambiguous definition of the three HB* hydrogens
  psfSegID PRA PRA PRA
  atomNameResidueRange HB1 2-2
  atomNameResidueRange HB2 2-2
  atomNameResidueRange HB3 2-2
}
```

This flexibility allows precise control over which atoms contribute to each collective variable.

Sources: [examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in](examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in#L5-L25), [examples/03_orientation.colvars.in](examples/03_orientation.colvars.in#L5-L10)

## Bias and Restraint Block Syntax

Bias and restraint blocks define potentials applied to collective variables to steer simulations or calculate free energies. The most common are `harmonic` (standard harmonic restraint), `harmonicWalls` (one-sided harmonic walls), and advanced methods like `abf` (adaptive biasing force) and `metadynamics`.

**Harmonic Restraints**: The simplest bias, applying a quadratic potential ½K(ξ - ξ₀)² where ξ is the colvar value, ξ₀ is the center, and K is the force constant.

```
harmonic {
  colvars myDistance      # Apply to this colvar
  centers 5.0            # Restraint center ξ₀
  forceConstant 10.0     # Force constant K
}
```

**Harmonic Walls**: One-sided restraints that penalize values beyond specified thresholds. Each colvar can have upper walls, lower walls, or both.

```
harmonicWalls {
  colvars NOE_1 NOE_2    # Apply to multiple colvars
  lowerWalls 3.5 4.2     # Lower thresholds
  lowerWallConstant 30.0 # Force constant for lower walls
  upperWalls 4.5 4.9     # Upper thresholds
  upperWallConstant 20.0 # Force constant for upper walls
}
```

**Bias Block Common Elements**: All bias blocks require:
- A `name` parameter (optional but recommended)
- A `colvars` parameter listing which collective variables to bias
- Bias-specific parameters (force constants, centers, etc.)

Multiple biases can be applied to the same collective variable, with forces summing appropriately. This enables complex protocols like umbrella sampling combined with metadynamics.

Sources: [examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in](examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in#L32-L58), [examples/03_orientation.colvars.in](examples/03_orientation.colvars.in#L17-L24)

## Data Types and Units

Colvars configuration supports several data types with appropriate unit conventions that must be understood for correct usage.

**Numeric Types**: 
- Integers for atom numbers, residue numbers, counts
- Real numbers (double precision) for distances, angles, force constants

**Distance Units**: All distances are specified in Ångströms (Å). This applies to collective variable values, boundaries, and widths.

**Angle Units**: All angles are specified in radians unless otherwise noted. Degrees must be converted (π radians = 180°).

**Energy Units**: Force constants are typically specified in kcal/mol/Å² for distance variables, but the effective units depend on the collective variable type. The `width` parameter provides implicit unit scaling.

**Special Data Types**:
- Quaternions (four-dimensional vectors) for orientation variables
- Quaternion format: `(w, x, y, z)` or space-separated values
- No explicit units (dimensionless)

```
# Orientation restraint using quaternion
harmonic {
  colvars Orient
  centers (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)  # Unit quaternion (no rotation)
  forceConstant 500.             # kcal/mol (quaternions dimensionless)
}
```

Sources: [examples/03_orientation.colvars.in](examples/03_orientation.colvars.in#L17-L24), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L85-L95)

## Configuration File Organization

Effective configuration file organization improves readability and maintainability. While the parser is flexible, following conventions helps avoid errors.

**Recommended Order**:
1. Global settings (output frequencies, analysis flags)
2. Collective variable definitions (colvar blocks)
3. Bias and restraint definitions (harmonic, ABF, metadynamics blocks)
4. Advanced analysis or output specifications

**Naming Conventions**:
- Use descriptive names for colvars: `distance_AB`, `angle_alpha`, `coord_num_water`
- Group related colvars with prefixes: `distance_ligand_core`, `distance_ligand_site`
- Name biases to reflect their purpose: `restraint_umbrella`, `bias_metad`

**Modular Configuration**: For complex simulations, consider splitting configuration into multiple files and using the MD engine's include mechanism to combine them. This is particularly useful when the same colvar definitions are used across different biasing protocols.

> [!TIP]
> Always validate your configuration file by running a short test simulation before starting production runs. The parser will catch syntax errors and unknown keyword issues early, saving computational resources.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L40-L60), [examples/README.md](examples/README.md#L1-L8)

## Error Handling and Troubleshooting

The Colvars parser provides detailed error messages to help diagnose configuration problems. Understanding these messages is crucial for efficient debugging.

**Common Errors**:
- **"Error: keyword XXX is required"**: A required parameter is missing from a block
- **"Error: found more than one instance of XXX"**: Duplicate keyword definitions
- **"Parse error: reached the end while looking for closing brace"**: Unbalanced braces
- **"Error: improper or missing value for XXX"**: Value format is incorrect

**Validation Approach**:
1. Check that all braces are balanced (each `{` has a matching `}`)
2. Verify keyword spelling (case-insensitive but spelling matters)
3. Ensure required parameters are present for each block type
4. Validate that values have appropriate types (numbers, strings, etc.)
5. Confirm that colvar names referenced in biases are defined

**Debugging Tips**:
- Start with a minimal configuration and add complexity incrementally
- Use the output log to see which parameters were actually read
- Check that atom selections are returning the expected number of atoms
- Verify units and scales (particularly for force constants and widths)

Sources: [colvarparse.cpp](src/colvarparse.cpp#L150-L200), [colvarparse.cpp](src/colvarparse.cpp#L750-L850)

## Complete Example: NOE Restraints Configuration

The following example combines all syntax elements into a realistic configuration for applying NMR-derived NOE restraints:

```
# Global settings
colvarsTrajFrequency 100
colvarsRestartFrequency 1000

# First NOE distance (intramolecular)
colvar {
    name NOE_1
    
    distanceInv {
        exponent 6
        
        group1 {
            # Three ambiguous hydrogens on residue 2
            psfSegID PRA PRA PRA
            atomNameResidueRange HB1 2-2
            atomNameResidueRange HB2 2-2
            atomNameResidueRange HB3 2-2
        }
        group2 {
            psfSegID PRA
            atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
        }
    }
    
    width 0.2  # Characteristic fluctuation
}

# Second NOE distance (intermolecular)
colvar {
    name NOE_2
    
    distanceInv {
        exponent 6
        
        group1 {
            # Four protein chains, same residue
            psfSegID PRA PRB PRC PRD
            atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
            atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
            atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
            atomNameResidueRange HE 11-11
        }
        group2 {
            # Drug molecule hydrogen
            psfSegID DRUG
            atomNameResidueRange H102 1-1
        }
    }
    
    width 0.2
}

# Restraint using harmonic walls
harmonicWalls {
    name walls_NOE
    colvars NOE_1 NOE_2
    
    # Experimental bounds
    lowerWalls 3.5 4.2
    lowerWallConstant 30.0   # kcal/mol/Å²
    upperWalls 4.5 4.9
    upperWallConstant 20.0   # kcal/mol/Å²
}
```

This configuration demonstrates:
- Global output frequency settings
- Two colvar definitions with atom group selections
- Ambiguous atom handling
- Multi-colvar bias application
- Comment usage for documentation

Sources: [examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in](examples/01_NOE_restraints.colvars.in#L1-L58)

## Next Steps

Now that you understand the basic configuration syntax, you're ready to explore more advanced topics:

- **[Core Architecture and Design Patterns](5-core-architecture-and-design-patterns)**: Understand how Colvars implements these configurations internally
- **[Distance-Based Variables](6-distance-based-variables)**: Learn about the various distance-based collective variable components
- **[Harmonic Restraints and Walls](11-harmonic-restraints-and-walls)**: Dive deeper into restraint methodologies and applications

The configuration syntax covered here forms the foundation for all Colvars usage. Practice with simple configurations using the provided examples in the `examples/` directory, then gradually add complexity as you become comfortable with the syntax and behavior.


# Core Architecture and Design Patterns



This page documents the fundamental architecture and design patterns that underpin the Colvars library, providing a structural understanding essential for extending or deeply integrating the codebase. The architecture follows a **layered design** with clear separation of concerns, enabling the library to be integrated into multiple MD engines while maintaining core functionality independent of implementation details.

## Architectural Overview

The Colvars library is organized into four primary architectural layers: the **Core Module** that orchestrates all operations, the **Collective Variable Layer** that defines and computes CVs, the **Bias Layer** that implements enhanced sampling methods, and the **Proxy Layer** that abstracts MD engine interfaces. This separation allows the core computational logic to remain engine-agnostic while providing standardized integration points for NAMD, LAMMPS, GROMACS, VMD, and other simulation packages.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "MD Engine Layer"
        NAMD[NAMD]
        LAMMPS[LAMMPS]
        GROMACS[GROMACS]
        VMD[VMD]
    end
    
    subgraph "Proxy Layer"
        Proxy[colvarproxy<br/>Engine Abstraction]
        ProxyAtoms[colvarproxy_atoms]
        ProxySystem[colvarproxy_system]
        ProxySMP[colvarproxy_smp]
    end
    
    subgraph "Bias Layer"
        Bias[colvarbias<br/>Base Class]
        ABF[colvarbias_abf<br/>ABF]
        Meta[colvarbias_meta<br/>Metadynamics]
        Restraint[colvarbias_restraint<br/>Restraints]
        Grid[colvargrid<br/>Grid Operations]
    end
    
    subgraph "Collective Variable Layer"
        Colvar[colvar<br/>CV Container]
        CVC[colvar::cvc<br/>CVC Base Class]
        Distance[distance<br/>CVC]
        Angle[angle<br/>CVC]
        RMSD[rmsd<br/>CVC]
        NN[neuralNetwork<br/>CVC]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Module"
        Module[colvarmodule<br/>Central Orchestrator]
        Types[colvartypes<br/>Math Types]
        Parse[colvarparse<br/>Configuration Parser]
        Deps[colvardeps<br/>Feature Dependencies]
    end
    
    NAMD -->|extends| Proxy
    LAMMPS -->|extends| Proxy
    GROMACS -->|extends| Proxy
    VMD -->|extends| Proxy
    
    ProxyAtoms -.-> Proxy
    ProxySystem -.-> Proxy
    ProxySMP -.-> Proxy
    
    Proxy --> Module
    Module --> Colvar
    Module --> Bias
    
    Colvar --> CVC
    CVC --> Distance
    CVC --> Angle
    CVC --> RMSD
    CVC --> NN
    
    Bias --> ABF
    Bias --> Meta
    Bias --> Restraint
    Bias --> Grid
```

Sources: [colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L76-L722), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L53-L722), [colvarbias.h](src/colvarbias.h#L22-L379), [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L549-L722)

## Core Module Architecture

The `colvarmodule` class serves as the **central orchestrator** of the entire library, managing the lifecycle of all objects and coordinating the main computational loop. It maintains collections of collective variables and biases, handles configuration parsing, and manages state I/O operations. The module follows a **singleton pattern** conceptually, with a single main instance accessible through the static `main()` method [colvarmodule.h#L957-L960](src/colvarmodule.h#L957-L960). This design ensures centralized control over the simulation state and provides a single point of access for configuration and queries.

### Computational Workflow

The module implements a well-defined computational workflow executed each simulation step:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Engine as MD Engine
    participant Proxy as colvarproxy
    participant Module as colvarmodule
    participant Colvar as colvar
    participant CVC as cvc
    participant Bias as colvarbias
    
    Engine->>Proxy: update_input()
    Proxy->>Module: update_engine_parameters()
    Module->>Colvar: calc_colvars()
    Colvar->>CVC: read_data()
    CVC-->>Colvar: calc_value()
    CVC-->>Colvar: calc_gradients()
    Colvar-->>Module: CV values ready
    Module->>Bias: calc_biases()
    Bias->>Colvar: get CV values
    Bias-->>Colvar: apply forces
    Module->>Colvar: update_colvar_forces()
    Colvar->>CVC: apply_force()
    Module->>Proxy: update_output()
    Proxy->>Engine: atomic forces
```

The workflow begins with the proxy updating input data from the MD engine, followed by collective variable computation. Biases are then calculated and forces are applied, with the final step communicating forces back to the MD engine through the proxy [colvarmodule.h#L624-L640](src/colvarmodule.h#L624-L640).

Sources: [colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L624-L640), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L299-L335)

### Type System and Mathematical Foundation

The module defines a **template-based type system** that provides compile-time control over numerical precision. The fundamental types include `cvm::real` for floating-point numbers (defaulting to `double`), `cvm::rvector` for 3D vectors, `cvm::matrix2d` for 2D matrices, and `cvm::quaternion` for rotations [colvarmodule.h#L136-L271](src/colvarmodule.h#L136-L271). The `colvarvalue` class provides a **polymorphic container** for different value types (scalars, vectors, quaternions) with automatic type conversions, enabling collective variables to have different dimensionalities while maintaining a unified interface.

Sources: [colvartypes.h](src/colvartypes.h), [colvarvalue.h](src/colvarvalue.h)

## Collective Variable Layer

The collective variable layer implements the **Strategy Pattern**, where the base `colvar` class defines the interface and `colvar::cvc` (collective variable component) classes implement specific computational strategies. This design allows new types of collective variables to be added without modifying existing code, simply by creating a new CVC subclass.

### Component Architecture

Each `colvar` object can contain **multiple CVCs**, which are combined according to polynomial combinations with configurable coefficients and exponents [colvarcomp.h#L84-L88](src/colvarcomp.h#L84-L88). This enables complex collective variables to be constructed from simpler building blocks. For example, a dihedral angle CV might be implemented using distance CVCs combined with trigonometric functions, or a coordination number might be expressed in terms of multiple distance components.

The `colvar::cvc` base class defines the interface that all components must implement:
- `calc_value()` - Compute the component's scalar or vector value
- `calc_gradients()` - Compute derivatives with respect to atomic coordinates
- `apply_force()` - Apply a collective variable force to atoms
- `calc_force_invgrads()` - Calculate total force from system atomic forces
- `calc_Jacobian_derivative()` - Compute Jacobian for phase space corrections

Sources: [colvarcomp.h](src/colvarcomp.h#L69-L303), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L592-L663)

### Available CVC Implementations

The library provides a comprehensive set of pre-implemented CVCs covering common collective variable types:

| Category | CVC Classes | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| **Distance-based** | `distance`, `distance_vec`, `distance_dir`, `distance_inv`, `distance_z`, `distance_xy` | Interatomic distances, projections, and inverse powers |
| **Angular** | `angle`, `dihedral`, `polar_theta`, `polar_phi`, `euler_theta`, `euler_psi`, `euler_phi` | Bond angles, torsions, and spherical coordinates |
| **Coordination** | `coordnum`, `selfcoordnum`, `groupcoordnum`, `h_bond` | Coordination numbers and hydrogen bonding |
| **Structural** | `rmsd`, `gyration`, `inertia`, `inertia_z`, `eigenvector` | RMSD, radius of gyration, moment of inertia |
| **Orientation** | `orientation`, `orientation_angle`, `orientation_proj` | Rotational alignment and projection |
| **Advanced** | `neuralNetwork`, `torchANN`, `customColvar`, `linearCombination` | Neural networks, custom functions, combinations |
| **Path-based** | `CartesianBasedPath`, `CVBasedPath`, arithmetic/geometric path variants | Path collective variables and string methods |

Sources: [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L597-L653), [colvarcomp_distances.cpp](src/colvarcomp_distances.cpp), [colvarcomp_angles.cpp](src/colvarcomp_angles.cpp)

### Force Computation Chain

Force computation follows a **reverse-mode automatic differentiation** pattern, where forces propagate from biases through collective variables down to individual atoms:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Bias Force<br/>F_bias] --> B[colvar::update_forces_energy]
    B --> C[colvar::update_extended_Lagrangian]
    C --> D[colvar::communicate_forces]
    D --> E[colvar::cvc::apply_force]
    E --> F[atom_group]
    F --> G[Individual Atoms]
    
    style A fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
    style D fill:#bbf,stroke:#333
    style G fill:#bfb,stroke:#333
```

The `colvar` class manages the force application through its `update_forces_energy()` method, which handles extended Lagrangian dynamics when enabled and ultimately calls `communicate_forces()` to distribute forces to atoms [colvar.h#L358-L365](src/colvar.h#L358-L365). Each CVC's `apply_force()` method then transforms the collective variable force into atomic forces based on the computed gradients.

Sources: [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L358-L365), [colvarcomp.h](src/colvarcomp.h#L172-L181)

## Bias Layer Architecture

The bias layer implements the **Template Method Pattern** combined with the **Strategy Pattern**. The base `colvarbias` class defines the workflow for bias computation, while derived classes implement specific biasing algorithms (ABF, metadynamics, harmonic restraints, etc.).

### Base Class Template

The `colvarbias` class establishes the computation template through virtual methods that derived classes override:

- `update()` - Main entry point called each step
- `calc_energy()` - Compute the bias potential energy
- `calc_forces()` - Compute forces on collective variables
- `communicate_forces()` - Send forces to the colvar objects

The base class maintains pointers to the collective variables it biases and caches their values and forces [colvarbias.h#L295-L307](src/colvarbias.h#L295-L307).

Sources: [colvarbias.h](src/colvarbias.h#L22-L330)

### Grid-Based Biases

Many biases (ABF, metadynamics, histogram reweighting) use multidimensional grids for storing probability distributions, free energy estimates, or bias potentials. The `colvargrid` class hierarchy provides **templated grid containers** with support for different data types (scalar values, gradients, counts) and automatic handling of periodic boundary conditions:

- `colvar_grid_scalar<T>` - Grids of scalar values
- `colvar_grid_gradient<T>` - Grids storing gradients  
- `colvar_grid_count<T>` - Grids for histogram counts

Grids are associated with collective variables and automatically handle binning operations based on CV values and widths [colvarbias.h#L19-L33](src/colvarbias.h#L19-L33).

Sources: [colvargrid.h](src/colvargrid.h), [colvarbias_ti.h](src/colvarbias_ti.h#L361-L375)

### Bias Hierarchy

The bias classes form an inheritance hierarchy that reuses common functionality:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class colvarbias {
        <<abstract>>
        +update()
        +calc_energy()
        +calc_forces()
        #colvars: vector~colvar*~
        #colvar_values: vector~colvarvalue~
        #colvar_forces: vector~colvarvalue~
    }
    
    class colvarbias_ti {
        <<template>>
        +update()
        #ti_system_forces: vector~colvarvalue~
        #ti_avg_forces: colvar_grid_gradient*
        #ti_count: colvar_grid_count*
    }
    
    class colvarbias_abf {
        +update()
        #samples: colvar_grid_count*
        #gradients: colvar_grid_gradient*
        #pmf: colvar_grid_scalar*
    }
    
    class colvarbias_meta {
        +update()
        #hills: vector~hill~
        #bias_gradient: colvar_grid_gradient*
    }
    
    class colvarbias_restraint {
        +update()
        #centers: vector~colvarvalue~
        #force_constants: vector~colvarvalue~
    }
    
    class colvarbias_histogram {
        +update()
        #histogram: colvar_grid_count*
    }
    
    colvarbias <|-- colvarbias_ti
    colvarbias_ti <|-- colvarbias_abf
    colvarbias <|-- colvarbias_meta
    colvarbias <|-- colvarbias_restraint
    colvarbias <|-- colvarbias_histogram
```

The `colvarbias_ti` class provides common functionality for thermodynamic integration-based biases (like ABF) with grid-based force averaging [colvarbias_ti.h#L336-L379](src/colvarbias_ti.h#L336-L379). Specialized biases like ABF and metadynamics extend this with their specific algorithms.

Sources: [colvarbias.h](src/colvarbias.h#L336-L379), [colvarbias_abf.h](src/colvarbias_abf.h), [colvarbias_meta.h](src/colvarbias_meta.h)

## Proxy Interface Pattern

The **Proxy Pattern** is central to Colvars' ability to integrate with multiple MD engines. The `colvarproxy` class defines a virtual interface that abstracts all engine-specific operations, allowing the core Colvars code to remain completely independent of the hosting program.

### Proxy Composition

The proxy interface is composed through multiple inheritance, with each base class handling a specific aspect of engine interaction:

| Proxy Component | Responsibility | Key Methods |
|----------------|----------------|-------------|
| `colvarproxy_system` | System parameters (timestep, PBC) | `dt()`, `request_total_force()`, `position_distance()` |
| `colvarproxy_atoms` | Individual atom data | `init_atom()`, `get_atom_position()`, `apply_atom_force()` |
| `colvarproxy_atom_groups` | Atom group operations | `init_atom_group()`, `get_atom_group_com()`, `apply_atom_group_force()` |
| `colvarproxy_volmaps` | Volumetric maps | Access to grid-based potential maps |
| `colvarproxy_smp` | Parallel computing | `smp_loop()`, `smp_thread_id()`, `smp_lock()` |
| `colvarproxy_replicas` | Multi-replica communication | `replica_comm()`, `replica_index()` |
| `colvarproxy_script` | Scripting interface | `run_force_callback()`, `run_colvar_callback()` |
| `colvarproxy_io` | I/O operations | `log()`, `error()`, file I/O methods |

The main `colvarproxy` class inherits from all these components using **multiple inheritance**, creating a unified interface [colvarproxy.h#L549-L560](src/colvarproxy.h#L549-L560).

Sources: [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L44-L722)

### Engine-Specific Implementations

Each MD engine implements a concrete proxy class that inherits from `colvarproxy` and overrides virtual methods with engine-specific code:

- `colvarproxy_namd` - NAMD integration
- `colvarproxy_lammps` - LAMMPS integration  
- `colvarproxy_gromacs` - GROMACS integration
- `colvarproxy_vmd` - VMD integration

These implementations are located in the engine-specific directories (`namd/`, `lammps/`, `gromacs/`, `vmd/`) and handle details like accessing NAMD's `AtomID` objects, LAMMPS atom arrays, or GROMACS coordinate arrays.

Sources: [README.md](README.md), [namd/colvarproxy_namd.h](namd/colvarproxy_namd.h)

### Data Flow Through Proxy

The proxy manages two-way data flow between the MD engine and Colvars:

**Input Flow** (Engine → Colvars):
1. `update_input()` called at each MD step
2. Atom positions read from engine into proxy buffers
3. `colvarmodule::calc_colvars()` computes CV values
4. CV values used by biases to compute forces

**Output Flow** (Colvars → Engine):
1. Biases compute forces on CVs
2. `colvar::communicate_forces()` distributes to atoms
3. Forces accumulated in proxy's `atoms_new_colvar_forces` buffer
4. `update_output()` sends forces back to MD engine

The proxy maintains atom data in structured arrays (`atoms_positions`, `atoms_total_forces`, `atoms_new_colvar_forces`) that can be efficiently accessed by both the proxy and Colvars code [colvarproxy.h#L264-L278](src/colvarproxy.h#L264-L278).

Sources: [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L627-L633)

## Feature Dependency System

Colvars implements a sophisticated **feature-based dependency system** through the `colvardeps` class. This system allows components to declare capabilities (features) and automatically enable/disable dependencies, ensuring that required computations are performed without manual coordination.

### Feature Declaration

Each class (colvar, cvc, bias) maintains a static vector of `feature` objects that describe available functionality. Features are identified by integer IDs and have names, descriptions, and dependency relationships:

```cpp
static std::vector<feature *> cvc_features;
static std::vector<feature *> cv_features;  
static std::vector<feature *> cvb_features;
```

For example, enabling the `f_cv_total_force` feature automatically enables dependencies like `f_cv_gradient` and `f_cv_collect_gradients` [colvardeps.h](src/colvardeps.h).

### Dependency Resolution

When a feature is enabled through `enable()`, the system traverses the dependency graph and recursively enables all required features. This **topological dependency resolution** ensures that all necessary computations are prepared. Features also define **side effects** through `do_feature_side_effects()`, which perform initialization when a feature is first enabled.

Sources: [colvardeps.h](src/colvardeps.h), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L95-L117)

### Feature Categories

Features are organized into several categories:

- **Computation features** - Control what is calculated (values, gradients, total forces)
- **I/O features** - Control output (trajectory, energy, restart files)
- **System features** - Require system capabilities (total forces, periodic boundaries)
- **Optimization features** - Enable performance optimizations (parallelization, scaling)

This system provides **fine-grained control** over computation costs while ensuring correctness through automatic dependency management.

Sources: [colvardeps.h](src/colvardeps.h)

## Configuration and Parsing Architecture

Configuration parsing follows a **declarative approach** where objects are constructed from configuration strings. The `colvarparse` class provides the foundation for keyword-based configuration parsing.

### Parsing Workflow

Configuration proceeds through multiple stages:

1. **Read Configuration** - `colvarmodule::read_config_file()` or `read_config_string()` loads the configuration
2. **Global Parameters** - `parse_global_params()` extracts module-wide settings
3. **Collective Variables** - `parse_colvars()` creates and initializes colvar objects
4. **Biases** - `parse_biases()` creates bias objects

The parsing system uses **keyword-value pairs** with support for nested blocks and comments. Each class implements its own parsing logic by calling helper methods like `get_keyval()` to extract typed values [colvarparse.h](src/colvarparse.h).

Sources: [colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L431-L470), [colvarparse.h](src/colvarparse.h)

### Backward Compatibility

The configuration system includes mechanisms for maintaining **backward compatibility** with older configuration files. The `append_new_config()` method allows new configuration to be generated during parsing to implement compatibility transformations [colvarmodule.h#L463-L466](src/colvarmodule.h#L463-L466).

## State Management and Serialization

The state management system enables **checkpointing and restart** capability through a comprehensive serialization framework. Each major class implements methods for reading and writing its state:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[colvarmodule] -->|write_state| B["Formatted Stream[]"]
    A -->|write_state| C["Binary Stream()"]
    B --> D["Text Restart File"]
    C --> E["Binary State Buffer"]
    
    D -->|read_state| A
    E -->|read_state| A
    
    style B fill:#bbf,stroke:#333
    style C fill:#fbb,stroke:#333
```

The system supports both **formatted (text)** and **unformatted (binary)** serialization through overloaded methods [colvarmodule.h#L544-L577](src/colvarmodule.h#L544-L577). The text format is human-readable for debugging, while binary format provides efficiency for frequent checkpointing.

State data is organized hierarchically, with the module coordinating serialization of all colvars and biases. Each object contributes a block of labeled data that can be independently parsed [colvarbias.h#L143-L237](src/colvarbias.h#L143-L237).

Sources: [colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L544-L577), [colvarbias.h](src/colvarbias.h#L143-L237)

## Parallel Computing Architecture

Colvars supports multiple forms of parallel computing through the `colvarproxy_smp` interface:

### SMP Parallelization

Symmetric multiprocessing parallelization uses **OpenMP** or engine-specific threading to parallelize independent computations:

- **CVC-level parallelization** - Different CVCs within a colvar can be computed in parallel
- **Bias-level parallelization** - Different biases can be evaluated simultaneously
- **Inner loop parallelization** - Repetitive operations (e.g., distance calculations) can be parallelized

The proxy provides `smp_loop()` which distributes iterations across threads [colvarproxy.h#L478-L478](src/colvarproxy.h#L478-L478).

Sources: [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L459-L509)

### Multi-Replica Communication

The `colvarproxy_replicas` interface enables communication between multiple simulation replicas for methods like **multiple-walker metadynamics** or **replica exchange**. Each replica has an index and can send/receive data to other replicas [colvarproxy_replicas.h](src/colvarproxy_replicas.h).

## Memory Management and Optimization

### Smart Pointer Usage

Modern CVC implementations use `std::shared_ptr<colvar::cvc>` for component storage, enabling **automatic memory management** and safe sharing of component references [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L666-L666). This represents an evolution from earlier raw pointer usage.

### Reference Counting for Atoms

The proxy implements **reference counting** for atoms and atom groups to avoid redundant data storage. An atom used by multiple colvars is stored once with a reference count incremented each time it's requested [colvarproxy.h#L264-L268](src/colvarproxy.h#L264-L268). This optimization reduces memory overhead and data transfer costs.

### CUDA/HIP Support

When compiled with CUDA or HIP support, the proxy uses **custom allocators** (`CudaHostAllocator`) for atom arrays that allocate pinned (page-locked) memory, improving data transfer performance between host and GPU [colvarmodule.h#L90-L123](src/colvarmodule.h#L90-L123).

Sources: [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L666-L666), [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L264-L268)

## Extension Points for Developers

The architecture provides several well-defined extension points:

### Adding New Collective Variable Components

To add a new CVC type:

1. Create a class inheriting from `colvar::cvc`
2. Implement required virtual methods (`calc_value()`, `calc_gradients()`)
3. Register in the component type map using `add_component_type()`
4. Add configuration parsing in the constructor

See existing implementations in `colvarcomp_*.cpp` files for examples.

### Adding New Bias Types

To add a new bias:

1. Create a class inheriting from `colvarbias` or an intermediate base
2. Implement `calc_energy()`, `calc_forces()`, `update()`
3. Add state serialization if needed
4. Register in `colvarbias::get_global_bias_map()` pattern

See `colvarbias_abf.cpp` or `colvarbias_meta.cpp` for examples.

### Creating Engine Integrations

To integrate with a new MD engine:

1. Create a class inheriting from `colvarproxy`
2. Implement all virtual methods for engine interaction
3. Create engine-specific code for initialization and callback handling
4. Test all CVCs and biases with the new integration

> [!TIP]
> The proxy interface is the key to engine integration - focus on implementing efficient methods for accessing atom positions and applying forces, as these are called every step and dominate performance.

## Design Pattern Summary

| Pattern | Location | Purpose |
|---------|----------|---------|
| **Singleton** | `colvarmodule` | Single coordinator instance |
| **Strategy** | `colvar::cvc` hierarchy | Interchangeable CV computation algorithms |
| **Template Method** | `colvarbias` base class | Fixed bias computation workflow |
| **Proxy** | `colvarproxy` interface | Engine abstraction layer |
| **Factory** | Component type maps | Dynamic object creation from config |
| **Observer** | Feature dependency system | Reactive computation enabling |
| **Composite** | `colvar` with multiple CVCs | Building complex CVs from simple ones |
| **State** | State serialization | Checkpointing and restart |

Sources: [colvarmodule.h](src/colvarmodule.h#L76-L960), [colvar.h](src/colvar.h#L53-L722), [colvarbias.h](src/colvarbias.h#L22-L379), [colvarproxy.h](src/colvarproxy.h#L549-L722)

## Further Reading

For deeper understanding of specific aspects:
- Learn about distance-based variables in [Distance-Based Variables](6-distance-based-variables)
- Understand angular and dihedral variables in [Angular and Dihedral Variables](7-angular-and-dihedral-variables)
- Explore the proxy interface details in [Proxy Interface and Engine Integration](20-proxy-interface-and-engine-integration)
- Study parallel computing support in [Parallel Computing and SMP Support](24-parallel-computing-and-smp-support)

# Distance-Based Variables



Distance-based variables represent one of the most fundamental categories of collective variables in Colvars, enabling the measurement and control of spatial relationships between atoms, groups of atoms, or molecular centers. These variables form the building blocks for complex enhanced sampling simulations, allowing researchers to monitor ligand-receptor binding distances, protein-ligand proximity, inter-domain separations, and many other distance-dependent phenomena. For beginners, mastering distance-based variables provides essential groundwork for understanding more complex collective variable types and building sophisticated free energy calculations.

Sources: [colvarcomp.h](src/colvarcomp.h#L328-L346), [colvarcomp_distances.cpp](src/colvarcomp_distances.cpp#L20-L90)

## Architecture Overview

The distance-based variable architecture follows an object-oriented design where each specific distance type inherits from a common base class. This hierarchical structure enables code reuse, consistent interfaces, and extensibility. At the foundation lies the `cvc` (collective variable component) base class, which provides core functionality like value calculation, gradient computation, and force application. All distance-based variables extend this foundation, implementing their specific geometric calculations while maintaining a unified API for the simulation engine.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class cvc {
        <<base class>>
        +calc_value()
        +calc_gradients()
        +apply_force()
        +dist2()
        +wrap()
    }
    
    class distance {
        +group1: atom_group
        +group2: atom_group
        +dist_v: rvector
        +calc_value()
        +calc_gradients()
    }
    
    class distance_vec {
        +calc_value() returns vector
        +apply_force()
        +dist2_lgrad()
        +dist2_rgrad()
    }
    
    class distance_dir {
        +calc_value() returns unit vector
        +apply_force()
    }
    
    class distance_z {
        +main: atom_group
        +ref1: atom_group
        +axis: rvector
        +fixed_axis: bool
    }
    
    class distance_xy {
        +dist_v_ortho: rvector
    }
    
    class distance_inv {
        +exponent: int
        +calc_value() returns 1/r^n
    }
    
    cvc <|-- distance
    distance <|-- distance_vec
    distance <|-- distance_dir
    cvc <|-- distance_z
    distance_z <|-- distance_xy
    cvc <|-- distance_inv
```
